docs.title: How to Contribute
docs.text:
1. Clone the repo and install dependencies (see the README).
  2. Edit or create a .md file inside docs/.
  3. Push to main — the site rebuilds and deploys automatically in ~1–2 minutes.

Quick edits without cloning

Every page has a :material-pencil: edit button (top right) that opens the file directly in GitHub's web editor.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: Document theorems, lemmas, proof sketches, conjectures, and other insights here. Each entry should be self-contained enough that someone unfamiliar with the day-to-day context can understand what was shown, how, and why it matters.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Understand where AI-assisted mathematical discovery currently stands
  • Meet with Dr. Srinivasan (my mentor) and other collaborators to establish a working plan for the summer.
  • Figure out which open problems in the group's focus areas (approximation algorithms, online algorithms, learning theory) are feasible to make progress on this summer.
  • Begin learning Lean

docs.title: Approach and Implementation
docs.text:
I spent the first two days prompting AI models directly on candidate problems to get a feel for what kinds of results might realistic to potentially make progress on over the summer. On Wednesday I read up on recent AI-for-math results, like OpenAI's discrete geometry result and DeepMind's work on AlphaEvolve to understand the current state of the art in AI-assisted discovery.

Thursday I met with the grad student I will be working with for the rest of the summer, Javier, to discuss how we will work together. Friday I met with my mentor, Javier, and another professor we will be working with, Dr. Binghui Peng. The professors suggested that we spend the next few weeks reading papers in the group's areas and identifying open directions worth pursuing. I also started learning a little bit of Lean. Additionally, to keep track of all the different possible directions we could take, Dr. Peng suggested we create some way to track all the papers and work we do. So, I also looked into the various ways to track our work, settling upon a GitHub Pages / MkDocs research site, for which I created a repository.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Working plan for the summer: paper-reading weeks followed by focused efforts on specific open problems and conjectures.
  • Started reading Shi Li's 1.488-Approximation for the Uncapacitated Facility Location Problem.
  • Started learning basic Lean.
  • Created repository for MkDocs site.

Overall, it was a solid orientation week. Most of the value came from narrowing down our direction rather than actual technical output.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Website setup is a standing task that will continue most weeks going forward.

docs.title: Week 2
docs.text:
Dates: 06-08 to 06-14

// PUT THIS IN WEEK TWO and set up the group's GitHub Pages / MkDocs research site.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Read Shi Li's facility location paper.
  • Create the setup for the GitHub Pages with MkDocs site
  • Begin reading Bhangale–Zhang's 4.509-Approximation for Generalized Min Sum Set Cover (GMSSC).

docs.title: Approach and Implementation
docs.text:
This week established the general schedule for the next three weeks: - Monday spent reading the paper to grasp the core problem and gain a general understanding of their approach - Tuesday meeting with Javier to discuss the paper - Wednesday spent on exploring what progress might be possible - Thursday meeting with Javier again to check in and updating the website - Friday meeting with mentors to report the week's progress and set the next week's reading.

I read and understood the facility location paper, but found the GMSSC problem more interesting so moved towards its paper instead. I worked through the LP relaxation setup, including why the natural LP generalization from ordinary Min Sum Set Cover fails and how KC-style inequalities are used in its place. I also spent time Monday through Wednesday learning a little bit of Lean, and finished the Glimpse of Lean exercises. Lastly, I created the initial website setup this week, and added the initial set of papers and articles that the professors have provided to it.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Understood the general premise of Shi Li's facility location paper.
  • Started the GMSSC paper, worked through the LP setup and the motivation for the KC inequalities.
  • Continued learning Lean.
  • Set up the MkDocs site and updated it with the provided resources.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Although I've understood GMSSC's LP setup quite well, the rounding technique remains to be read in detail, so I plan to return to it for a deeper read later in the summer once I've read a few more papers and have more background.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Read Bahmani, Mehta, and Motwani's Online Graph Edge-Coloring in the Random-Order Arrival Model.
  • Specifically investigate Conjecture 3.12: the non-negativity of a recursively defined sequence \(c_\ell\) underlying the paper's near-optimal \(K\)-round competitive ratio claim.

docs.title: Approach and Implementation
docs.text:
Over the weekend, Dr. Srinivasan recommended that Javier and I look into Conjecture 3.12 in Bahmani, Mehta, and Motwani's Online Graph Edge-Coloring in the Random-Order Arrival Model, and soon after, Dr. Peng let us know that ChatGPT actually came up with a proof for the conjecture. With that in mind, I spent Monday and Tuesday reading and understanding the paper. Tuesday, I met with Javier and we looked over the ChatGPT-provided proof for the conjecture, coming to the agreement that ChatGPT's proof is indeed correct.

Wednesday and Thursday, I spent doing a little more Lean and helping re-write the proof for Conjecture 3.12. Friday I again met up with both professors, and we discussed the progress for this week and decided to keep going with the paper-reading and problem-exploration for next week.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Resolved Conjecture 3.12, establishing the non-negativity of the \(c_\ell\) sequence needed for the paper's claim that \(K = O(\log(\Delta/\log n))\) rounds gives a competitive ratio of \(1 + O(1/\log K) + o(1)\).
  • Finished the learning the basics of Lean this week.

This was the strongest technical result of the summer so far. The conjecture was explored at the recommendation of Dr. Srinivasan, the proof was found by Dr. Binghui prompting ChatGPT, and then verified by Javier and I.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: No notes for this week.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Begin exploring Euclidean Ramsey theory problems.
  • Read Szyfelbein's Constant Factor Approximation for the Uniform Decision Tree problem.

docs.title: Approach and Implementation
docs.text:
Since I'm on UMD's campus, I happened to meet the students of the REU program here (UMD CAAR), and since I knew the professor of the Ramsey Theory group, I got to listen to some talks about Ramsey Theory. In particular, Euclidean Ramsey Theory piqued my interest as an area to explore for AI-assisted math. This was early on in the week of 06-22 to 06-28. On Tuesday, July 23, I wasn't able to meet with Javier, but I was able to meet Dr. Binghui in-person. During the meeting, he suggested that I look into learning theory as its one of his areas of focus. That's what I continued exploring on Wednesday.

However, Thursday and Friday I couldn't do any work due to some housing problems, although I was able to make the meeting with my mentor and Javier.

The housing problems continued onto the beginning of next week. However, around Tuesday evening, I started to work through Szyfelbein's paper for the uniform decision tree problem. Then, I met with Javier on Thursday and we realized that we have a lot more time available to meet and work. We also decided that he is going to explore Euclidean Ramsey Theory more in-depth while I work on the learning theory papers. Thus, from next week and on, we will be meeting at least three times a week for a few hours each day to work together. Friday, July 4th, was a holiday so we didn't meet.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Worked through the constant-factor approximation for the uniform decision tree problem.
  • Explored Euclidean Ramsey theory a little bit.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: • This is a joint entry of two weeks for one week because I faced some housing issues due to which the middle part of these two weeks were very unproductive

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Read Blanc, Lange, Qiao, and Tan's Open Problem: Properly learning decision trees in polynomial time?
  • Return to the GMSSC paper for a slightly deeper read.

docs.title: Approach and Implementation
docs.text:
I worked to try and gain a general understanding of the various discussions and approaches to the open problem being discussed. Over Monday and Tuesday, I got a decent grasp of the problem and the current state of the art. Since learning theory is a brand new area for me, I had to get a lot of background knowledge as I read through the problem and current state. Then, on Wednesday, Javier expalined to me the work he had been doing with Euclidean Ramsey Theory and we had a quick meeting with Dr. Srinivasan. He suggested that we look at the GMSSC paper again, and so I focused on that for the next two days. Javier came to the conclusion that the AI agent was not doing well with Euclidean Ramsey Theory and we should focus on the other problems we have.

When I returned to the Bhangale–Zhang GMSSC paper for a deeper pass, I focused specifically on the kernel transformation and the LP-rounding process, as that's where they actually made their progress. I did not finish it, though, so I will continue to understand it more next week.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Read most of the foundations for the decision tree open-problems paper.
  • Came to the conclusion that, for now, we should shift our focus away from the Euclidean Ramsey Theory problems.
  • Returned to the GMSSC paper.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: • GMSSC deep-dive is ongoing and will likely carry into next week.
